hints.content: To determine the point on the unit circle that corresponds to angle $\theta$, we start from the point $(1,0)$ and move counterclockwise along the circle until the angle that is formed between our position, the origin, and the positive $x$-axis is equal to $\theta$.

Let's take point $A$. The angle it forms with the positive $x$-axis must be acute, so $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ would be an appropriate value for it.

options.alt: A unit circle on an x y coordinate plane where the center of the unit circle is at the origin and the circumference of the circle touches (one, zero), (zero, one), (negative one, zero), and (zero, negative one). Point A is located at near two o'clock on the circle. Point B is located near eight o'clock on the circle. Point C is located near five o'clock on the circle. A line segment extends from (zero, zero) to point A. An angle from the arc starting at (one, zero) and opening counter clockwise to point A has an angle measurement of pi over six radians.

hints.content:
Point $B$ forms with the positive $x$-axis an angle that is slightly larger than $\pi$, so an appropriate value is $\dfrac{8\pi}{7}$.

A line segment extends from (zero, zero) to point B. An angle from the arc starting at (one, zero) and opening counter clockwise to point B has an angle measurement of eight pi over seven radians.

hints.content:
Point $C$ forms with the positive $x$-axis an angle that is between $\dfrac{3\pi}{2}$ and $2\pi$, so an appropriate value is $\dfrac{5\pi}{3}$.

A line segment extends from (zero, zero) to point C. An angle from the arc starting at (one, zero) and opening counter clockwise to point C has an angle measurement of five pi over three radians.

hints.content:
In conclusion, this is the correct answer:

Point | Angle
:-: | :-:
$A$ | $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$
$B$ | $\dfrac{8\pi}{7}$
$C$ | $\dfrac{5\pi}{3}$
